text.p: MARK FEATURE
By Mike Dolan

LONDON, Nov 4 (REUTER) - The Bundesbank is playing a dangerous game with a foreign exchange market which is desperate for volatility and long of dollars, but currency analysts said the authorities will be prepared to counter any blowout.

A dollar/mark break back below supports just under 1.50 is likely to be met with verbal protests from Bundesbank and French authorities, covert intervention from central banks across Europe and, if weakness persists, talk of further German easing.

"If we continue to see the dollar weakening under 1.50 we would expect to at least see some comments from the likes of the Bundesbank and French Treasury protesting the move," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets.
"When you see the economic data released this week, the last thing the German authorities want now is a rising mark."
The problems in managing the situation are all about timing and fine-tuning of policy expectaions at a very sensitive time.

Investors flush with the third-quarter success of high-yield European bond plays, funded partly by cheap yen borrowings, are now looking to book those profits as the year-end nears. The rise of the yen this week is both an ominous warning signal that this is underway and a potential catalyst.
Unless the European authorities are careful, the risk of exaggerating this unwinding of positions could prompt another destabilising dash for marks in Europe.
The dollar's dip to close to 1.50 marks overnight should have sent warning lights flashing, said analysts.

"The dollar/yen story has come to an end for now but dollar/mark is much better protected and will have a lot of central bank support under 1.50," said ABN Amro economist Tony Norfield. The mark/yen cross rate, as a result, looks "absolutely dreadful," he said.
Policy-wise, however, the Bundesbank is tightrope walking without a safety net.

On one hand, it is trying to juggle volatile interest rate expectations at the turn of an economic cycle, while at the same time acting as a vocal quality-control inspector in the moulding of the final stages of European monetary union.
Doing both without boosting the mark is a tricky business.

The problem is another sustained shift to marks from current levels would risk a trend reversal in dollar/mark, potentially destabilise the whole process of European monetary union and squeeze the life out of the fragile German export-led recovery.

Analysts said that in a environment in which domestic price pressures are minimal, unemployment is rising and fiscal policy across Europe is being strangled, only conspiracy theorists could find a reason why the Bundesbank would want this.

"The Bundesbank has been happy the economy is out of deflationary territory, but it must tread a fine line between a sensible monetary policy for domestic reasons and the pressures that can build on the FX markets," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
The big question is that at what point does the Bundesbank feel the return to marks will become too risky to tolerate.

The dollar is the key. A drop below 1.50 marks would be worrying, not least because of the technical picture that would paint. For example, the dollar's 200-day moving average is currently at 1.5035 and a rising trendline in place for more than year cuts in at 1.4925.
"If dollar/mark goes down to 1.45, German business confidence could collapse...it would devastating for the export-led German recovery," said Prendergast at Merrill.
"The Bundesbank may not have a case for a rate cut unless the FX market forces them to do so, but if push comes to shove the Bundesbank may well ease again."
